AJK.name: Juneau
AJK.excerpt: LONG TERM.../Wednesday through Friday/... With the most impactful weather in the rear-view, winds across the panhandle begin to diminish through Wednesday.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: Wind advisory has been expanded to the Ketchikan area, with all wind advisories moved up from 6 PM tonight start time to beginning now. Northeast to easterly wind gusts have been observed in the Ketchikan and Metlakatla area, particularly near Ward Cove, Saxman, and a few sites on Annette Island above 500 ft. Looking to see these winds transition from northeasterly and easterly to more southeasterly and increasing during the day as the front moves up from the south.

sections.name: Synopsis
paragraphs: - Fog and Freezing fog continue for the central panhandle into this morning creating difficult travel conditions.

- A stronger low pressure system moves north into the southeastern Gulf of Alaska Monday, increasing winds across the southern inner channels and the offshore Gulf of Alaska coastal waters into Tuesday.
- An associated front with the Gulf of Alaska low pressure system moves into the southern Panhandle Monday increasing rain chances Monday into Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: / through Sunday night / A low south of the gulf of Alaska will be rotating a band of rain and wind north into the southeast gulf and into the panhandle then starting north through the panhandle. Wind gusts to 40 to 45 mph for the coastal communities. Gusts mostly for the Prince of Wales Island and possibly Metlakatla region to Tuesday morning. Chances of rain to start then to Categorical overnight and into the start of Tuesday, Snow may mixed in or be the precipitation type for the northern panhandle or north central. Accumulations are expected to be on the light side.

LONG TERM.../Wednesday through Friday/... With the most impactful weather in the rear-view, winds across the panhandle begin to diminish through Wednesday. Rain is likely to continue due to a series of fronts moving through the area, but winds are expected to diminish to less than 20kts in the inner channels, and less than 30kts in Lynn Canal, Clarence Strait, and coastal Gulf waters. A series of about 3 or 4 fronts are expected to track across the panhandle from Wednesday through Saturday night bringing light to moderate rain, but are expected to be seasonable. With low pressure moving through the gulf and high pressure established over the Yukon and British Columbia, a stronger east/west gradient sets up across the panhandle. Winds are likely to be east to northeast in direction through much of this time with east/west oriented channels likely to see channeling of winds.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: A weak system will move into the area on Thursday, bringing valley rain and mountain snow. Precipitation amounts with this system will be light. A cold front will graze the region on Friday bringing moderate snows to the mountains into Saturday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Light valley rain and mountain snow showers expected through this afternoon.
- Dry conditions on Tuesday with valley fog developing overnight.
- Unsettled weather will return Wednesday through the end of the week alongside warmer temps and higher snow levels.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A shortwave ridge will transition over the area tonight and Tuesday, with partial clearing and patchy fog developing overnight. Southwest flow aloft ahead of an approaching system will shift the surface winds to E-SE over the higher terrain. This will push low clouds and stratus toward the Lower Treasure Valley into Baker County, along the I-84 corridor. Slight improvement in fog and stratus on Tuesday afternoon in these areas. The system will weaken as it moves inland bringing increased clouds and showers late Tuesday into Wednesday morning. Showers will mainly be confined to eastern OR, and the west central ID mountains on Wednesday morning before tapering off during the afternoon.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A weak system will move into the area on Thursday, bringing valley rain and mountain snow. Precipitation amounts with this system will be light. A cold front will graze the region on Friday bringing moderate snows to the mountains into Saturday. Current forecast does not reflect this system. Upper level ridging returns for Sunday and Monday with fog and low stratus possible in the valleys.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Forecast confidence remains very low by the end of the forecast period. Guidance generally keeps a very active subtropical jet near the region, with another chance of mountain snow early next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A quick-hitting storm system will bring a round of mountain snow showers this afternoon and evening, with travel impacts possible across Park and Summit counties. A few light rain and snow showers are also possible across the Palmer Divide and adjacent plains.
- A gradual warming trend likely through the rest of the week, with quiet weather expected through Thanksgiving
- Next storm system could bring some snow to the central and northern mountains Friday into Saturday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: It isn't often the case that the lowest confidence forecast period is the near term (next 12-24 hours). However, this is the case today as a weak trough drifts across the state through tonight.

There is considerable uncertainty in how this afternoon/evening's mountain snow showers play out. While CAMs were very bullish with precipitation potential as recently as the 12z cycle, there has been a notable downtrend since then. Regional/global deterministic guidance hasn't not changed significantly, and supports at least light snow across the mountains beginning in a few hours. One may be wondering, "why the Winter Weather Advisory?" Today's forecast and advisory are almost entirely driven by favorable ingredients for heavy snow showers that could have travel impacts despite relatively light snowfall amounts in the grids. Very steep lapse rates (close to 8-9C/km through the lowest 6km) and modest mid- level convergence/lift, combined with efficient snow ratios could lead to brief periods of 1-2"/hr snowfall rates. It's possible that these snow showers stick mainly to the Mosquito Range, but any snow showers that reach the I-70 corridor could lead to brief but difficult travel conditions through this evening. Essentially this an impacts-driven advisory with a low floor but high ceiling in terms of travel impacts through the early overnight hours.

We still look on track to enter a period of mild and dry weather for the rest of the week. A weak ridge is expected to develop to our west on Tuesday, leading to a drier northwesterly flow aloft. The ridge should slowly shift eastward and flatten by mid-week while a strong cutoff low develops over the Ohio River valley. Temperatures on Tuesday and Wednesday should return to the upper 40s to low 50s across the plains. Mid to upper 50s are likely for Thanksgiving, with additional warming possible to end the week.

Forecast confidence decreases on Friday and Saturday as a broad swath of moisture embedded in west-northwesterly flow moves towards the forecast area. This moisture is embedded in an area of stronger flow aloft, located between a broad trough in south central Canada and a strong ridge to the west of Baja California. There has been poor consistency (both model to model and d[model]/dt) in this period, with the ECMWF generally further south with the jet and accompanying moisture/lift, while the GFS is on the drier side. This is also reflected across their respective ensemble distributions. Interestingly, the AIGEFS has shifted notably away from the physics-based GFS/GEFS today, though it's not clear if this is an actual trend or run-to-run noise. I have a slight preference towards the wetter (snowier) solutions that would likely bring at least some minor travel impacts to the mountains for the start of the weekend.
Forecast confidence remains very low by the end of the forecast period. Guidance generally keeps a very active subtropical jet near the region, with another chance of mountain snow early next week.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Monday...A fast moving shortwave trough aloft will sweep eastward across our counties, and with adequate mid level moisture, will produce orographic snows for our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Elevated winds are possible Tuesday afternoon through the night for the wind prone areas of southeast Wyoming.
- Another round of even stronger winds and more widespread is possible Thursday into Friday.
- Significant forecast uncertainty exists for the weekend due to an unusually large range of possible forecast outcomes.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Very chilly day across the region as low clouds have remained mostly socked in, keeping temperatures around or below freezing. The exceptions to this have been along the I-80 corridor from Arlington through Cheyenne where breaks in the clouds have allowed for some sunshine, and temperatures have jumped into the mid to upper 30's. Aloft, a trough is passing across the Rockies with the strongest and most impactful portion of this feature well to our south in the southern Four Corners area. Because of this with the best instability and moisture to our south, the majority of this feature will not produce any noteworthy precipitation activity outside of some very light snow in the mountains.

Moving into Tuesday, we'll become enveloped in split flow aloft as the troughing to the south begins to deepen as it moves into the Central US while a new low over Canada dives down into the Dakotas. Under this pattern, we'll see pressure gradients tighten with an elongated jet feature develop and stretch over the US. While the strongest portions of this jet will be associated with the respective features creating it, we'll still see our region under a stronger northerly flow aloft that will fuel enhanced surface winds for the day. In house guidance still isn't excited enough that we should see High Wind Warning level criteria with probabilities only maxing around 40% for the Arlington area at the highest, but stronger gusts of around 40-55 mph are possible with an errant gust or two nearing that threshold of 58+ mph. Otherwise it'll be a dry day with no precipitation expected as highs recover east of the Laramie Range, increasing by around 10 degrees. Some morning fog could still linger for areas of Converse, Niobrara, Platte, and Goshen Counties, but increasing winds and drier air should help to alleviate this by later Tuesday morning.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Wednesday...Ridging aloft will keep it dry with relatively light winds. 700 mb temperatures near 1 Celsius will yield high temperatures in the 40s.

Thanksgiving...The next shortwave trough aloft moves from eastern Montana and eastern Wyoming in the morning, to the western high plains by evening. This system is moisture starved with only perhaps some mid and high level cloudiness. Low and mid level gradients suggest a breezy to windy day. More mild downwind of the Laramie Range and I-25 due to downslope warming. Continued cold to the west of I-25.

Friday...Looks like the beginning of a windy weekend with strong northwest flow aloft and deep unidirectional flow in the atmosphere. Will likely see high winds for our typically wind prone locations such as Arlington, Bordeaux and the I-80 Summit, with strong winds possibly in nearby locations of southeast Wyoming as well. Enough low and mid level moisture for orographic snows across the Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges. Despite the winds, it will remain relatively mild with 700 mb temperatures near -4 Celsius yielding high temperatures in the 40s west of I-25, with low to mid 50s east of I- 25.

Saturday...Strong west northwest flow will occur in the low and mid levels, and looking like a more widespread high wind event for much of southeast Wyoming and parts of the Nebraska Panhandle. Again, looks like adequate mid level moisture for orographic snows across the northern Laramie, Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges. Will see a slow cooling trend over the weekend based on 700 mb temperatures.

Sunday...The flow aloft turns westerly though still remains strong enough at low and mid levels for windy conditions across the wind prone locations. A surface high across the central Plains states will slide across our eastern counties, to the east of I-25, with winds lessening.

Monday...A fast moving shortwave trough aloft will sweep eastward across our counties, and with adequate mid level moisture, will produce orographic snows for our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges. Temperatures similar to Sunday, in the 40s west of I-25, with upper 40s to mid 50s further east.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: A deep, yet fast ridge develops during the mid-week, bringing an end to precipitation region-wide. This precedes a late-week system passing through the western CONUS, with the likeliest arrival sometime on Friday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A quick-moving system is bringing snow to the mountains and some mountain valleys today with snowfall totals of 2 to 6 inches with locally higher amounts.
- Travel conditions through passes could become very difficult at times. A Winter Weather Advisory is in effect for the San Juan Mountains and central Colorado mountains over 9,000 feet.
- Active weather remains possible late Thanksgiving week, but some details still remain uncertain. Stay tuned for updates to timing and impacts as they become available.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: Snow accumulations are anticipated to sit between 2 and 4 inches across the central Colorado mountains, but slick roads combined with increased holiday traffic poses the risk for challenging conditions. Due to the possibility for difficult travel over passes in these areas, we have now issued a Winter Weather Advisory for Colorado zones 10 and 12. This will last until 11 PM tonight.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A fast-moving trough is making its way through the region today, bringing with it another round of active weather. Looking at cameras across the region, locations around and in the San Juans have started to see impactful snow over the past several hours with some areas sitting around 2-3 inches. Most roadways through the San Juans are either wet or covered in snow at this point in time, so expect for travel to be difficult at times should you be driving through. By the time storms have moved out of southwestern Colorado, snow accumulations are anticipated to sit around 3-6 inches, though should banded snow develop, higher accumulations cannot be ruled out. The possibility of stronger snow bands is low to moderate at this time though primarily due to lacking instability in areas northeast of the Four Corners. Nonetheless, brief heavy snow rates remain in the realm of possibility. We've already seen visibility drop to a quarter mile in some areas due to snowfall, so even without heavy snow rates, reduced visibility may develop at several locations. Due to the already-present impacts across the San Juans combined with increasing holiday travel, we have opted to issue a Winter Weather Advisory for the San Juans above 9,000 feet until 6PM today in spite of sub-advisory snow forecasts.

Throughout the course of the day, look for the bulk of active weather to shift northeastwards into the central Colorado mountains. Some CAM's remain bullish on moderate snowfall rates making their way into the Sawatch Mountains and potentially over Vail Pass, but we lean towards a middle-of-the-road outcome in regards to snow accumulations, with snow totals at and below pass level around I-70 resting below 4 inches. Due to Thanksgiving travel ramping up though, even this amount of snow could cause issues during travel, especially given how impactful precipitation has been on major roadways over the past couple weeks. Be weather aware and be prepared for tougher-than-normal travel conditions today.
ANOTHER ROUND OF SNOW AFTER THANKSGIVING:

A deep, yet fast ridge develops during the mid-week, bringing an end to precipitation region-wide. This precedes a late-week system passing through the western CONUS, with the likeliest arrival sometime on Friday. Unfortunately, deterministic models are still struggling to come to an agreement on the nature of this storm. What is apparent is the development of high pressure off the SoCal coast and split flow across the Intermountain West. Where this split flow and resulting quieter weather occurs is highly uncertain at this point. Should it dip far enough south for strong northwesterly flow to establish itself over the CWA, we could see favorable orographics support snowfall over the Park Range. This looks to be the most likely scenario at this time, but with the upper-level pattern being so complex, there is too little confidence to bank on this outcome coming to fruition. That being said, the probability of snowfall during the late-week period is increasing, and so if you are planning to travel during this time, be prepared for the possibility of difficult travel conditions, especially over the northern Colorado mountains and maybe even across other portions of the CWA as well. Stay tuned over the coming days for additional updates.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Transitory ridging builds across the region into Wednesday, leading to dry conditions and warming temperatures, with latest operational and ensemble model continuing to indicate eastern Pacific energy splitting as it translates across the Intermountain West Thursday and Friday, keeping the region in moderate northwest flow into the end of the Thanksgiving Holiday weekend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Passing weather system to bring quick bursts of moderate to heavy snow across the higher terrain into portions of the southeast plains tonight.
- Trending warmer and drier into the Thanksgiving Holiday Weekend.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Current water vapor imagery and upper air analysis has increasing southwest flow aloft across the region as a broad upper trough continues to dig across the Great Basin. Regional radars increasing echoes along and west of the Continental Divide, with some echoes also developing across the higher terrain the Sangres at this time. Partly to mostly cloudy skies have helped to kept temperatures on the cool side, with readings in the 40s across the plains and mainly in the 20s and 30s across the higher terrain at this time.

Current model data remains in good agreement of said upper trough digging into the Four Corners region through the late afternoon, and then lifting out across the Rockies through the overnight hours and into the High Plains into Tuesday morning. Steep lapse rates, along with increased uvv associated with a couple jet core lifting out across south central and southeast Colorado will bring bands of moderate to heavy snowfall into the Continental Divide this afternoon, with the bands continuing to lift out across the higher terrain into the southeast plains through the evening and into the over night hours. Higher impacts from these bands of snow, with quick bursts of 1 to 2 inches per hour possible, have prompted short fused Winter Weather Advisories (based on possible impacts and not total snow amounts) across the Continental Divide, as well as the Sangre de Cristo mountains into the southern I-25 Corridor with the potential for additional snow squall warnings being issued through the evening. Some higher res model data also indicate to potential for bursts heavy snow across portions of the San Luis Valley, the Wet Mtn Valley and across portions of the the Lower Arkansas River Valley, in which we will continue to monitor for possible additions to Winter Weather highlights as well possible snow squall warnings.

Precipitation and clouds diminish from west to east through the overnight hours into Tuesday morning, save for a few possible snow showers across the Central mountains, as drier and subsident northwest flow takes hold across the Rockies. Temperatures to remain below seasonal levels mainly in the 40s across the plains, and 30s and 40s across the higher terrain, save for 20s at the peaks.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Transitory ridging builds across the region into Wednesday, leading to dry conditions and warming temperatures, with latest operational and ensemble model continuing to indicate eastern Pacific energy splitting as it translates across the Intermountain West Thursday and Friday, keeping the region in moderate northwest flow into the end of the Thanksgiving Holiday weekend. This will keep chances of precipitation confined mainly to the Northern and Central Mtns, with temperatures remaining at and above seasonal levels. However, will need to continue to monitor the potential for surface high pressure building across the Northern High Plains to send a backdoor cold front into eastern Colorado later next weekend.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Around the end of November into early December, ensemble guidance continues to hint at a more active pattern raising PoPs in the forecast CWA-wide. However, numerous caveats exist with this forecast given large model spread down the line.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A mostly quiet weather pattern looks to persist as systems continue to move in from the west, then dip south after traversing the Sierra range.
- Temperatures are expected to run near normal through mid-week, then warming to 5-10F above normal through the remainder of November.

- A signal exists for a return to an active pattern starting December 1st, though many differences exist regarding trough placement which would significantly impact the forecast yielding great uncertainty.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Currently, a weak mid-level trough is traversing east across the Great Basin into the Southwest. Stronger ascent remains further south across AZ, keeping most of UT and southwest WY dry and cool. A light dusting of mountain snow looks to have occurred across our southern UT mountains, though dry air and lack of meaningful ascent has kept any precipitation confined much further south.

Transient ridging looks to develop across the Great Basin following this system with quiescent weather expected to persist through at least mid-week. Temperatures are expected to warm slightly through mid-week, though will remain near-normal each day. Conditions are forecast to remain dry and stable with terrain driven winds as a result.

Come Thursday, a strong ridge of high pressure looks to develop across the Eastern Pacific just off the coast of Baja California. Additionally, numerous mid-level troughs look to eject east into CA. Unfortunately, a split flow pattern looks to develop as this ridge will shift these troughs north initially, will result in these troughs digging south across the Sierra range into Southern CA and AZ. This will yield weaker ascent across the forecast area and keep colder mid-level temperatures further north resulting in less precipitation occurring across the forecast area, if at all. This pattern looks to persist through the end of November, keeping us dry for the most part. Some perturbations look to split north through the period yielding low PoPs across our northern UT high terrain (~30%) which could result in some light mountain snow and perhaps valley rainfall in the absence of meaningful large scale ascent.

Around the end of November into early December, ensemble guidance continues to hint at a more active pattern raising PoPs in the forecast CWA-wide. However, numerous caveats exist with this forecast given large model spread down the line. While frequent troughing is expected, ensemble guidance continues to struggle with trough placement and whether they dive south across the Sierra range or hold together further north. When looking at meteograms for snowfall across the Cottonwoods, it becomes evident that the models are rather uncertain yielding extreme differences in snowfall accumulations, potentially as low as 1" to 40". When diving into cluster analysis, it appears that the southern track is favored at this time with around 60% of all members supporting this solution. The forecast is expected to change as the month comes to an end, and this forecaster certainly hopes that the southern track does not continue to remain favored similar to last season.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: You can trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you on slopes steeper than about 30 degrees at higher elevations. The most dangerous slopes are those with wind-drifted snow that face west to north through east. If you experience audible collapsing or shooting cracks, give suspect slopes a wide buffer and stick to lower-angle terrain, as you can trigger avalanches from a distance or from below.
Slopes less than 30 degrees in wind-sheltered areas and slopes below treeline offer safer travel options.

2753.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: There's still a good chance you can trigger an avalanche on steep wind-drifted slopes facing northwest to north to east as you approach or enter the alpine. Fresh slabs formed over the weekend rest on well-connected weak layers in deeper areas and can fail from a distance away. By sticking to lower-angle, sheltered slopes, or more southerly aspects, you will lessen your odds of triggering a slide.

2754.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: Most slopes are generally safe from avalanches due to shallow or discontinuous snow cover. You might be able to trigger a small avalanche where recent winds have formed pockets of stiffened snow below ridgelines, on lee slopes, and around rocky outcrops in the alpine.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: Snow cover is still too thin for avalanches on most slopes. In the alpine, you should steer around hard drifts of snow on steep terrain features and below ridgetops. Unfortunately, the slopes with enough snow to ride are also where you might find enough snow for slides.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: The snow cover is too thin for slides on most slopes, so avalanche danger is LOW. Recent snow drifts rest on weak, old snow. If you find a continuous drift of firm snow on a steep terrain feature, you can trigger a small slide. Steer around drifted pockets of snow where you see them below ridges or inside gullies.
